summary.text: Statistical mechanics applies probability and statistics to huge numbers of microscopic particles to explain the properties of matter in bulk.
It explains temperature, pressure and heat capacity from microscopic behaviour, and it bridges exact mechanics and our incomplete knowledge by using an ensemble of possible states.
Maxwell's 1859 velocity distribution was the first statistical law in physics, Boltzmann built the field from the 1870s, and Gibbs formalized it in 1902.

items.prompt: A scientist wants the pressure of a room's air, which holds countless molecules. Why does she not simply track each one?

options.label: Air molecules hold perfectly still
Each one is unneeded, and cannot be known exactly
Pressure has nothing to do with molecules
Molecules exist only as a mathematical idea

items.explain: Everyday life does not require, and quantum mechanics does not allow, knowing every particle's exact position and momentum, so uncertainty about the state is added.

items.prompt: A physicist imagines a huge number of imaginary copies of one box of gas, each in a different microscopic state. What does this collection represent?

options.label: A probability distribution over the possible states
A list of every real gas box in the world
The one exact state the gas is in
A record of how the gas changed over time

items.explain: The statistical ensemble is a large collection of virtual copies in various states, serving as a probability distribution over all possible states.

items.prompt: Why does a balloon feel firm when you squeeze it, according to Bernoulli's picture of gases?

options.label: The gas is a solid jelly
The gas particles stick to the walls
Heat flows out through the rubber
Countless molecules keep hitting the surface

items.explain: Bernoulli argued that gases are great numbers of molecules moving in all directions, and their impacts on a surface cause the pressure we feel.

items.prompt: A chemist wants to model how fast a reaction proceeds, not only the final balance it reaches. Which part of the field helps?

options.label: Classical thermodynamics of equilibrium alone
Counting molecules by hand
Non-equilibrium statistical mechanics
The ensemble of a single particle

items.explain: Classical thermodynamics deals mainly with equilibrium, while non-equilibrium statistical mechanics models the speed of irreversible processes such as chemical reactions.

items.prompt: Gibbs's methods were worked out in classical mechanics. Why did they keep working when quantum mechanics arrived?

options.label: Quantum mechanics copied them exactly
They were so general that they adapted easily
They ignored the quantum state entirely
They were rewritten from scratch

items.explain: Gibbs's methods were of such generality that they adapted easily to quantum mechanics and still form the foundation of the field.

items.prompt: Maxwell studied what happens when gas molecules collide again and again. What did he argue about temperature?

options.label: Collisions equalize temperatures, so gases tend toward equilibrium
Collisions create hot and cold regions
Collisions stop once gas is at rest
Collisions make all molecules the same speed

items.explain: Maxwell gave the first mechanical argument that molecular collisions equalize temperatures, leading to a tendency toward equilibrium.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Statistical mechanics is a mathematical toolkit that uses probability and statistics to study huge collections of tiny particles. Its aim is to explain how matter behaves in bulk, starting from the physical laws that govern how atoms move. It also goes by the names statistical physics and statistical thermodynamics. Its methods have spread well beyond physics, into biology, neuroscience, computer science, information theory and even sociology.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is needed
paragraphs.text: Ordinary mechanics needs two things: the complete state of a system at one moment, and an equation of motion that carries that state forward in time. With both, any past or future state can in principle be worked out. But when we do something at the human scale, such as running a chemical reaction, we do not need the exact position and speed of every molecule, and in quantum mechanics knowing them is not even possible in theory. Statistical mechanics bridges this gap by accepting some uncertainty about which state the system is in.

paragraphs.heading: The ensemble
paragraphs.text: The key tool is the statistical ensemble: a large collection of imagined, independent copies of the system, each in a different state. Put another way, the ensemble is a probability distribution over all the states the system could be in. Each copy changes over time by the equation of motion, so the ensemble as a whole changes too. An ensemble that does not change over time is called an equilibrium ensemble, and its condition is called statistical equilibrium. That does not mean the particles have stopped moving; only the ensemble itself stays fixed.

paragraphs.heading: From particles to temperature
paragraphs.text: Statistical mechanics grew out of classical thermodynamics. There it accounted for large-scale properties, like heat capacity, pressure and temperature, using microscopic quantities that wobble around average values and follow probability distributions. Its equilibrium branch, statistical thermodynamics, tries to derive how materials behave thermally from their particles and the interactions between them. The non-equilibrium branch deals with ensembles that change over time, and it is used to model how fast processes driven by imbalances run, such as chemical reactions and flows of particles and heat.

paragraphs.heading: Roots in the study of gases
paragraphs.text: In 1738 the Swiss physicist and mathematician Daniel Bernoulli brought out Hydrodynamica, the groundwork for the kinetic theory of gases. He argued that a gas is a great many molecules moving in every direction, that their impacts on a surface make the pressure we feel, and that heat is just the kinetic energy of their motion. In 1859 the Scottish physicist Maxwell worked out how molecular velocities are spread, giving the share of molecules whose velocity falls in any given range. This was the first statistical law in physics.

paragraphs.heading: Boltzmann and Gibbs
paragraphs.text: In 1864 Boltzmann, then a young student in Vienna, read the paper Maxwell had written and spent much of his life building on it. His work in the 1870s started statistical mechanics, and he introduced the idea of an equilibrium ensemble. In 1902, shortly before his death, Gibbs published Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics, which set the subject out as a general approach for every mechanical system, large or small. Gibbs worked within classical mechanics, but his methods carried over easily to quantum mechanics and still underpin the field.
